title: Superposition and Measurement
description: One qubit is in a superposition of the states $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$. What quantum state will it be in after measurement in the 0/1 basis?
explanation: When we measure the qubit in the 0/1 basis, we receive an output of 0 or 1 and collapse the qubit to that state.
choices: The qubit will be in both state 0 and 1
The qubit will be in either state 0 or 1
The qubit will be in neither state 0 nor state 1
the qubit will remain in state 0 or state 1

title: Superposition and measurement
description: A qubit starts in an unknown superposition state. An H gate is applied, followed by a measurement in the 0/1 basis. How can the qubit be returned to its original unknown state after measurement?
explanation: Once we measure the qubit, we collapse the state, irreversibly changing it. It is not possible unless we can re-prepare the qubit in the initial state from scratch.
choices: Apply another H gate and measure again
Apply another H gate and do not measure
Measure the qubit again and then apply an H gate
It is not possible to recover the initial unknown state

title: Qubit measurement
description:
A qubit starts in the 0 state and then has an H gate applied to it. If we measure the qubit, what is the probability we find it in the state "0"?

You may wish to open the circuit simulator in another window to test the circuit before answering.
explanation: The Hadamard transforms the state to the $|+\rangle$ state, which is a 50/50 superposition of $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$.
choices: Between 1% and 49%
Between 51% and 99%

title: Qubit measurement
description:
A qubit starts in the 0 state and then has two H gates applied to it. If we measure the qubit, what is the probability we find it in the state "0"? You may use the histogram on the right panel to help answer this question.
You may wish to open the circuit simulator in another window to test the circuit before answering.
explanation: Two Hadamards cancel each other out, returning the qubit to the $|0\rangle$ state.
choices: Between 1% and 49%
Between 51% and 99%

title: Qubit measurement
description:
A qubit starts in the 0 state and then has two H gates applied to it with one T gate in the middle. If we measure the qubit, what is the probability we find it in the state "0"? You may use the histogram on the right panel to help answer this question.

You may wish to open the circuit simulator in another window to test the circuit before answering.
explanation: The T gate applies a phase of $\pi/4$ to the $\ket{1}$ component. This changes the state, and the second Hadamard no longer transforms the state exactly to the $\ket{0}$ state.
choices: Between 1% and 49%
Between 51% and 99%

title: Circuit comparisons
description: We have two qubits, both starting in the $\ket{0}$ state with two gates applied on each. Which statement about the two circuits is true?
explanation: These two circuits perform the same operation and both output the state $\ket{-}$, as can be seen by showing that $HX=ZH$.
choices: The first qubit is more likely to be found as "0" than the second qubit
The second qubit is more likely to be found as "0" than the first qubit
The output states are opposite superposition states
The output states of the circuit are the same

title: Circuit Representation
description: How would you express the below circuit in bra-ket notation? Note that the starting state is $\ket{0}$ by default.
explanation: You can think about both $YHZ\ket{0}$ and the circuit as starting with the state $\ket{0}$ and applying the gate $Z$, then $H$, then $Y$.
choices: $ZHY\ket{0}$
$YHZ\ket{0}$
$\ket{0}HYZ$
$\ket{0}ZHY$
$\bra{0}ZHY\ket{0}$
$\bra{0}YHZ\ket{0}$

title: Circuit Representation
description: Drag-and-drop gates to represent the circuit $TYX\ket{0}$.

title: Equivalent gates
description:
The $X$ gate switches $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$ components, like the classical NOT operation. Can you make an $X$ gate using only $H$ and $Z$? Drag and drop gates into the circuit to build your gate.
Recall that $Z$ applies a $\pi$ phase shift to the $\ket{1}$ component.
explanation: $HZH=X$. Another way to think about this is that the $Z$ gate flips the $\ket{+}$ and $\ket{-}$ states, so by transforming into the $+/-$ basis, we can use the $Z$ as a NOT operation.

title: Equivalent gates
description:
The $X$ gate switches $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$ components, like the classical NOT operation. Can you make an $X$ gate using only $H$ and $T$? Drag and drop gates into the circuit to build your gate.

Recall that $T$ applies a $\pi/4$ phase to the $\ket{1}$ component.
explanation: $TTTT=Z$. In other words, phases add up.
